paragraphs: A classifier's confidence can become unreliable when images differ from its training data. This paper studies that calibration problem through the geometry of the model's internal features. It asks how the size of a feature representation and its angular alignment with a classifier contribute to confidence when inputs change.

The proposed Geometric Sensitivity Decomposition separates these geometric quantities into components that depend on the individual input and components that do not. The input-dependent part captures information sensitive to changes in the image. The other part serves to reduce training loss without representing that sensitivity. From this decomposition, the authors derive a simple extension of softmax-linear models that learns to separate the two components during training.

Across several vision models, the resulting approach improves standard calibration measurements under distribution shifts and image corruption, with lower complexity than comparison methods. On corrupted CIFAR100, it reports a 30.8% relative improvement in Expected Calibration Error over the previous state of the art. The findings connect confidence reliability to how models organize their feature geometry.
neurips-2021-a-geometric-perspective-tow.tldr: Separating input-sensitive and input-insensitive feature geometry improves neural confidence calibration under distribution shifts and corruption.

paragraphs: When several source tasks are available, deciding how much each should contribute to a target task involves more than measuring similarity. The amount of data available for each task also affects what can be learned reliably. This paper develops a mathematical framework that incorporates both considerations when quantifying transferability.

The analysis considers a specific setup: models learned on different tasks are combined linearly to learn the target task. The optimal weights in that combination become the transferability measure. Their analytical form depends on sample sizes, model complexity, and source–target similarity. This connects the usefulness of a source model to both its relationship with the target and the statistical resources behind it.

The authors then use a parameterized model to make the measure applicable to practical learning tasks. They develop an alternating iterative training algorithm for deep networks that implements the theoretical ideas. Image classification experiments show improvements over existing transfer learning algorithms in multi-source and few-shot settings, supporting the value of jointly considering similarity and sample availability.
neurips-2021-a-mathematical-framework-fo.tldr: The paper quantifies source-task usefulness through combination weights that account for task similarity, sample sizes, and model complexity.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets multiple clients train a shared model without exchanging their raw data. Strong overall performance, however, does not itself describe whether the model works consistently across clients or satisfies fairness requirements within them. This paper makes those concerns explicit parts of the learning objective.

The authors formulate training as constrained optimization with several objectives, one prediction loss for each client. They focus on improving the worst-performing client while imposing fairness constraints on every client. A surrogate maximum function brings all client objectives into the optimization, and a gradient-based procedure seeks a Pareto solution: a tradeoff where improving one objective cannot come without worsening another.

The theoretical analysis establishes that the method can converge to a Pareto solution achieving the stated min-max performance criterion under the fairness constraints. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report advantages over baselines in both fairness and performance consistency. The contribution is a framework that treats client-level disparities as training requirements rather than leaving them outside the optimization problem.
neurips-2021-addressing-algorithmic-disp.tldr: A constrained federated learning framework improves worst-client performance while enforcing fairness requirements across clients.

paragraphs: Dataset bias can change what a learning algorithm predicts for an individual. This paper asks whether one can certify that a particular prediction would stay the same across a specified collection of biased datasets. The challenge is that this collection may contain an enormous, or even infinite, number of alternatives.

The authors focus on decision-tree learners and let users describe bias through programmable models. These descriptions can include flipped labels, missing data, combinations of different biases, and changes directed at a particular group. A symbolic technique evaluates the learner across the represented datasets, allowing the method to reason about their predictions without separately training a tree on every alternative.

The resulting certificate is pointwise: for a specific test input, every dataset covered by the bias model leads to the same prediction. Its scope therefore depends on the specified dataset changes and the input being checked. Evaluations on datasets commonly used in fairness research demonstrate that this approach is viable across a range of bias models.
neurips-2021-certifying-robustness-to-pr.tldr: Symbolic analysis certifies when a decision-tree learner gives the same prediction for a test point across programmable dataset biases.

paragraphs: Estimating a treatment's causal effect becomes difficult when an unobserved factor influences both treatment and outcome. Proxy causal learning addresses this problem using structured side information about the hidden factor. Its recovery guarantee depends on identifiability conditions, so the availability of proxies alone does not establish that the causal effect can be recovered.

The underlying procedure uses two regression stages. The first models relationships between treatments and proxies; the second uses that learned relationship to estimate how treatment affects outcomes in the context supplied by the proxies. This paper introduces the deep feature proxy variable method, DFPV, to handle high-dimensional variables and complex nonlinear relationships through neural network features.

DFPV outperforms recent proxy causal learning methods on challenging synthetic benchmarks, including settings with high-dimensional images. The authors also show how proxy causal learning applies to off-policy evaluation in confounded bandit problems, where DFPV performs competitively. Together, these results extend the practical reach of the proxy framework to richer data and policy evaluation.
neurips-2021-deep-proxy-causal-learning-.tldr: DFPV uses neural features to extend proxy causal learning to complex, high-dimensional data and confounded bandit policy evaluation.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to make learning a new task faster when only a few examples are available. This paper focuses on the regularizer used by the base learner, the component that learns each task. A regularizer shapes that learning process by influencing which solutions the learner favors beyond fitting the available examples.

The authors identify a restriction in recent deep-kernel approaches: although these methods achieve strong performance, their base-learner regularizers are not learned. They propose MetaProx, which learns a proximal regularizer for the base learner. The central change is therefore to make the regularization itself adaptable through meta-learning, expanding what can be learned about how to approach a new task.

The paper provides a theoretical convergence result for MetaProx and reports experimental evidence supporting its advantage. These are complementary contributions: the analysis addresses convergence of the proposed algorithm, while the experiments support its practical value. The stated findings motivate learned regularization as a useful component of learning from few examples, alongside the deep-kernel approaches that frame the problem.
neurips-2021-effective-meta-regularizati.tldr: MetaProx learns a proximal regularizer for few-sample task learning, with a convergence result and supporting experiments.

paragraphs: In competitive multi-agent learning, each agent must balance pursuing rewarding actions with exploring alternatives. Because agents learn simultaneously, that balance also affects whether their collective behavior settles down. This paper studies smooth Q-learning, a model that explicitly combines game rewards with the costs associated with exploration.

The main result concerns weighted zero-sum polymatrix games, a structured class of competitive interactions. With positive exploration rates, smooth Q-learning converges to the unique quantal-response equilibrium even when the learning agents differ. This equilibrium describes behavior under bounded rationality, incorporating exploration into how agents respond to one another. The guarantee is tied to the stated game class and exploration condition.

The authors also establish fast convergence regardless of the number of agents, without requiring parameter fine-tuning. Experiments in network zero-sum games illustrate these results. The findings support an algorithmic approach to equilibrium selection in competitive multi-agent systems: within this setting, the learning dynamics have a uniquely specified equilibrium toward which they converge.
neurips-2021-exploration-exploitation-in.tldr: Smooth Q-learning converges to a unique quantal-response equilibrium in weighted zero-sum polymatrix games with positive exploration rates.

paragraphs: Gaussian Cox processes model event locations using an underlying intensity function whose uncertainty is described through a Gaussian process. Learning that intensity from observed events requires Bayesian inference, which can be computationally demanding. This paper introduces an inference scheme based on a path-integral formulation of the model.

The method avoids discretizing the input domain into a grid. Its computational cost grows linearly with the number of observed events, and its dependence on the number of inducing points is lower than that of the compared state-of-the-art variational Bayesian schemes. It also accommodates a broad range of link functions, which connect the Gaussian process to the event intensity.

These properties are especially useful for multidimensional inputs, where many inducing points may be needed. On synthetic and real-world datasets, the authors report predictive accuracy comparable to reference methods while running tens of times faster. The results suggest that changing the inference formulation can substantially reduce computation while retaining similar predictive quality in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-fast-bayesian-inference-for.tldr: A path-integral inference scheme makes Gaussian Cox process learning substantially faster while preserving comparable predictive accuracy in experiments.

paragraphs: Learning-based steering systems must interpret images affected by changing conditions. Corruption can originate inside the sensing system, through noise or hardware abnormalities, or outside it, through lighting, weather, and visibility. This paper proposes a gradient-free adversarial training framework intended to improve robustness to those image changes.

The approach combines sensitivity analysis, an FID-based parameterization, and basis perturbations. These ingredients provide a way to characterize image changes and use them during training. Although autonomous steering is the central application, the authors also apply the approach to image classification and detection tasks relevant to self-driving cars.

The reported results show improvement on the original dataset as well as datasets containing multiple perturbations or previously unseen perturbations. The abstract reports gains of up to 87% and 77% for those latter two settings, respectively. Comparisons with other state-of-the-art techniques support the method's effectiveness. The findings indicate that training with the proposed perturbation framework can improve both ordinary-task performance and resilience to corruption in the evaluated applications.
neurips-2021-gradient-free-adversarial-t.tldr: A gradient-free training framework using sensitivity analysis and basis perturbations improves robustness to image corruption in driving-related vision tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies signals that stay constant within regions of a multidimensional grid but are observed with additive Gaussian noise. Its goal is to recover the regions themselves. That makes the task about identifying the underlying partition, beyond estimating a denoised signal value at each grid location.

The proposed procedure uses computationally efficient dyadic classification and regression trees. Under regularity conditions on region shapes, the authors prove consistent partition recovery. The error rate depends on noise variance, the complexity of representing the partition with recursive rectangular splits, the logarithm of grid size, and the inverse square of the smallest difference between neighboring regions.

Under stronger assumptions, the error bound no longer depends on that partition-complexity factor and reaches a minimax-optimal rate. This means the sharper rate matches the best worst-case rate for the relevant setting. The theoretical guarantees also extend to two other partition estimators. Simulations support both the analysis and the effectiveness of the dyadic-tree procedure for recovering partitions.
neurips-2021-lattice-partition-recovery-.tldr: A dyadic-tree procedure recovers constant-valued regions in noisy grids, with minimax-optimal error rates under stronger assumptions.

paragraphs: Vehicle routing becomes harder as the number of locations grows, and methods that work well on small instances can deteriorate at larger scales. This paper introduces a learning-augmented local search framework that repeatedly selects a manageable subproblem and delegates its improvement to an existing black-box solver.

The framework uses spatial locality to restrict each step to a linear number of candidate subproblems, avoiding an exponential collection. Choosing which candidate to improve is treated as a regression problem. A Transformer trained on generated problem instances learns this selection task, while the subsolver remains responsible for improving the selected portion of the routing solution.

For routing instances with sizes from 500 to 3000, the method accelerates state-of-the-art solvers by 10 to 100 times while maintaining competitive solution quality. Learned selection contributes a further 1.5 to 2 times speedup relative to heuristic or random selection. Results generalize across several routing distributions, variants, and solvers, supporting the usefulness of learning where to spend optimization effort.
neurips-2021-learning-to-delegate-for-la.tldr: Learning which routing subproblems to delegate accelerates large-scale vehicle routing solvers while retaining competitive solution quality.

paragraphs: Many matrix estimation problems seek low-rank solutions, but optimization can still require expensive decompositions of high-rank matrices. This paper addresses nonsmooth objectives, where progress on avoiding that expense has been slower than for smooth problems. It analyzes the extragradient method for standard convex relaxations of these tasks.

The main guarantee requires generalized strict complementarity, an objective expressible as a maximum of smooth functions, and initialization sufficiently close to an appropriate solution. Under these conditions, the method converges at a rate of O(1/t) using only two low-rank singular value decompositions per iteration. The analysis specifies a tradeoff between the decomposition rank and the radius of the permitted initialization region.

Experiments on nonsmooth low-rank matrix recovery tasks support the theory. With simple initializations, replacing full-rank decompositions by decompositions matching the ground-truth rank produces exactly the same iterates in the reported experiments. This links the computational savings to preservation of the optimization trajectory, while the formal convergence claim remains conditional on the stated structural and initialization requirements.
neurips-2021-low-rank-extragradient-meth.tldr: Under structural and warm-start conditions, extragradient optimization achieves O(1/t) convergence using only low-rank matrix decompositions.

paragraphs: Online learning often measures regret against the best individual expert, even when data can be adversarial. This paper studies two relaxations. Quantile regret compares performance against a majority of experts, while the semi-adversarial setting permits data that lie between fully adversarial behavior and independent, identically distributed sampling.

The authors construct separate root-logarithmic regularizers for follow-the-regularized-leader algorithms. These choices achieve minimax-optimal regret in both settings and can be understood as variants of NormalHedge. The contribution is therefore a pair of regularization designs with optimal worst-case guarantees for their respective learning paradigms.

The analysis also extends KL regret upper bounds to potentially uncountable expert collections with arbitrary priors, uniformly over target distributions. For finite expert classes, it supplies tight full-information lower bounds for quantile regret. In the semi-adversarial setting, the proposed algorithm adapts more quickly to the unknown constraint governing the data and obtains uniformly improved regret bounds over existing methods. These results address both achievable performance and the limits against which optimality is judged.
neurips-2021-minimax-optimal-quantile-an.tldr: New root-logarithmic regularizers yield minimax-optimal regret guarantees for quantile and semi-adversarial online learning.

paragraphs: An image photographed from a digital screen can differ from what a person perceives directly. This paper investigates the security implications of moiré patterns arising in that process. The authors argue that familiar capture artifacts can conceal changes that substantially affect a neural network's interpretation of an image.

Their Moiré Attack generates patterns by mimicking the process of photographing digital devices. This connects the attack's appearance to a physical image-formation phenomenon. Its proposed stealth comes from the possibility that people will interpret the resulting pattern as an ordinary camera artifact and consequently overlook its adversarial role.

In the reported digital experiments, the attack achieves 100.0% untargeted success and 97.0% targeted success with a noise budget of four. The authors also report strong transfer across models and robustness under various defenses. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the evaluated digital attack and identify screen photography as a potential source of deceptive visual artifacts. The stated results do not make every occurrence of moiré evidence of an attack.
neurips-2021-morie-attack-ma-a-new-poten.tldr: A digital attack that mimics screen-photography moiré patterns achieves high reported success while resembling a familiar capture artifact.

paragraphs: Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics adds noise during gradient-based training. Existing information-theoretic analyses can provide informative generalization bounds when that noise is isotropic, meaning it has the same variance in every direction. This paper asks whether changing the directional structure of the noise can improve such a bound.

The authors develop a new information-theoretic bound that permits optimization over noise covariance. They then use matrix analysis to characterize the optimum. When the prior and posterior are optimized jointly, and a constraint is imposed to maintain low empirical risk, the optimal covariance is the matrix square root of the expected gradient covariance.

This is a conditional result about optimizing the proposed bound while controlling training performance. It connects the preferred noise structure to variation in the gradients, rather than treating all directions identically. The authors interpret it as supporting noise close to the empirical gradient covariance. Empirical observations validate the presented constraint and results, providing support for the relationship derived in the analysis.
neurips-2021-optimizing-information-theo.tldr: Under joint prior–posterior optimization and a low-training-risk constraint, an SGLD generalization bound favors noise covariance tied to gradient covariance.

paragraphs: This paper studies model-based bandits and reinforcement learning with nonlinear function approximations. It shows that guaranteeing global convergence can be statistically intractable even for a one-layer neural network bandit with deterministic rewards. That finding motivates approximate local maxima as a more attainable target for the analysis.

The authors introduce Virtual Ascent with Online Model Learner, or ViOlin. For nonlinear bandits and reinforcement learning, they prove convergence to a local maximum with sample complexity depending only on the model class's sequential Rademacher complexity. Their results also yield global or local regret bounds in particular settings, including certain linear bandits and two-layer neural network bandits.

The algorithmic insight concerns how learned models guide exploration. Optimism can cause excessive exploration even with a two-layer neural model class. For reaching local maxima, maximizing the model's virtual return is sufficient if the model also predicts the real return's gradient and Hessian reasonably well. This condition connects successful local improvement to learning both the slope and curvature of the true objective.
neurips-2021-provable-model-based-nonlin.tldr: ViOlin provides local-convergence guarantees for nonlinear model-based learning by exploiting predicted return geometry.

paragraphs: For a moving robot, an object's detected shape matters partly because of how it relates to the robot's trajectory. Conventional box-overlap metrics describe detection accuracy around the object, but are not designed to capture that relationship. This paper proposes evaluating detections from the perspective of the moving agent.

The authors introduce Support Distance Error, or SDE, as an egocentric measure of 3D detection quality. Their analysis reveals that coarse bounding-box geometry limits quality under this measure. To provide a more accurate description, they represent objects using amodal star-shaped polygons and introduce StarPoly, a simple model that predicts those contours.

Experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset show that SDE better reflects the safety impact of detection quality than box Intersection-over-Union. StarPoly's estimated contours also consistently improve egocentric detection quality over recent 3D detectors in those experiments. The work connects the choice of evaluation metric with the choice of object representation: measuring geometry in relation to the agent exposes shortcomings that richer contours can address.
neurips-2021-revisiting-3d-object-detect.tldr: An agent-centered detection metric motivates richer object contours that improve measured 3D detection quality relevant to motion and safety.

paragraphs: Small adversarial changes to an agent's observations can disrupt a deep reinforcement learning policy. This paper introduces RADIAL-RL, a training framework designed to improve robustness against perturbations bounded by an lp norm. The focus is on agents that must continue making useful decisions when their inputs are deliberately altered.

RADIAL-RL is compatible with popular reinforcement learning algorithms, and the authors demonstrate it with deep Q-learning, A3C, and PPO. Across Atari, MuJoCo, and ProcGen benchmarks, the trained agents consistently outperform prior methods under attacks of varying strength. The authors also report greater training efficiency, making computational cost part of the practical comparison.

The paper separately introduces Greedy-Worst-Case Reward, or GWC, to evaluate robustness without tying the assessment to a particular attack method. GWC can be computed efficiently and is reported to estimate reward under the worst possible sequence of adversarial attacks well. This distinction matters because resilience to tested attacks and an estimate of worst-case reward provide different views of an agent's robustness.
neurips-2021-robust-deep-reinforcement-l.tldr: RADIAL-RL improves robustness and training efficiency under bounded input attacks, while GWC estimates worst-case adversarial reward.

paragraphs: Neural sequence-to-sequence models usually predict the next element from its surrounding context. Although flexible, they can need substantial training data and struggle with tests of compositional generalization. This paper explores a hierarchical alternative that models the relationship between source and target sequences through synchronous grammars.

The proposed grammar relates each node in a target tree to a subset of nodes in a source tree. Both trees are latent: training does not require them to be supplied as observed structures. Instead, the model marginalizes over them during learning. A neural parameterization shares parameters across combinatorial structures, removing the need to hand-design features for those structures.

The authors evaluate the approach on SCAN, a diagnostic navigation task testing compositional generalization, as well as style transfer and small-scale machine translation. They report respectable performance relative to standard baselines. The results support latent neural grammars as a workable alternative across these domains, while preserving the modest claim that the approach performs respectably rather than establishing universal superiority.
neurips-2021-sequence-to-sequence-learni.tldr: A neural synchronous grammar learns latent source–target hierarchies and performs respectably across several sequence transformation tasks.

paragraphs: Natural gradient methods use curvature information to guide training, offering a possible route to faster optimization than first-order methods. Their computational demands make approximations important. This paper introduces Tensor Normal Training, or TNT, an approximate natural gradient method that requires knowledge of the shape of the model's training parameters.

TNT approximates the probabilistic Fisher matrix using blockwise covariance of sampling-based gradients. Its key assumption is that these tensor-shaped gradients follow a tensor normal distribution. That assumption gives their covariance a Kronecker-separable structure, allowing a tractable Fisher approximation. The resulting memory use and computation per iteration are described as only slightly higher than for first-order methods.

In the reported experiments, TNT optimizes better than state-of-the-art first-order methods and comparably to the second-order methods KFAC and Shampoo. It also generalizes as well as first-order methods while using fewer epochs. These findings support the practical promise of its structured curvature approximation, with the tensor normal assumption providing the mechanism that keeps the calculation manageable.
neurips-2021-tensor-normal-training-for-.tldr: TNT uses a tensor normal gradient assumption to make natural-gradient training tractable, achieving strong optimization with modest per-iteration overhead.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving 3D scene from monocular video is under-constrained, so existing neural approaches rely on learned prior information about dynamic content. This paper introduces TöRF, which replaces those priors with measurements from a time-of-flight camera. The aim is to provide additional observational information for dynamic scene reconstruction.

The neural representation incorporates an image-formation model for continuous-wave time-of-flight cameras. It works with raw sensor measurements rather than processed depth maps. This design lets reconstruction account for the measurement process and address problems associated with low-reflectance regions, multipath interference, and the camera's limited range of unambiguous depth measurements.

The authors show improved reconstruction robustness when calibration is inaccurate and when scenes contain large motions. They also discuss the benefits and limitations of combining RGB and time-of-flight sensors available on modern smartphones. The central contribution is the integration of raw physical measurements into the neural scene representation, using the sensor model to improve reconstruction quality in the evaluated dynamic settings.
neurips-2021-torf-time-of-flight-radianc.tldr: TöRF integrates raw time-of-flight measurements into neural radiance fields to improve dynamic scene reconstruction.

paragraphs: Visual classifiers can become sensitive to backgrounds even when those backgrounds do not determine the correct label. This paper formalizes a learning setting in which inputs are generated from two underlying sets, with only one determining labels. That structure separates label-relevant variation from the accompanying context in the learning problem.

The authors derive a risk bound that splits into bias and error terms and has surprisingly weak dependence on the true labels. Guided by the bound, they propose an algorithm aimed at reducing the bias term. Its key resource is the ability to sample independently from the two sets, allowing the training procedure to vary their contributions separately.

Applied to visual classification, the approach enables training from datasets containing only one synthetic example per class. Across several standard real-world image benchmarks, the authors report robust context-agnostic performance and good transfer to real domains. Direct training on real-world data without their techniques produces classifiers brittle to background perturbations, supporting the value of explicitly separating label information from context in this setting.
neurips-2021-towards-context-agnostic-le.tldr: A learning framework that independently varies label-determining content and context supports robust classification from minimal synthetic examples.

paragraphs: This paper asks how qualification disparities can persist between groups without assuming inherent group differences. Its model starts with groups that differ only in their initial qualification rates. Individuals receive classifications based on a real-valued feature and may subsequently change their qualification by imitating successful strategies within their own isolated group.

The classifier is Bayes-optimal and repeatedly retrained on the whole population. Group qualification rates evolve according to a replicator equation representing the imitation process. Within this model, the authors show that uniform classifier deployment can sustain differences indefinitely at nontrivial equilibrium states. Thus, repeatedly optimizing prediction across the population can coexist with persistent differences in the populations being classified.

The authors simulate commonly proposed fairness interventions and a new feedback-control mechanism capable of permanently eliminating qualification-rate disparities in the modeled system. The result concerns evolving qualification itself, rather than only equality in classification decisions. Its interpretation depends on the modeled feedback loop, including isolated within-group imitation and the repeated deployment of globally trained classifiers.
neurips-2021-unintended-selection-persis.tldr: A dynamic model shows how initially unequal qualification rates can persist under optimal classification and explores interventions that remove them.

paragraphs: A useful reinforcement learning representation should discard irrelevant information while preserving what an agent needs to choose optimal actions. Mutual-information maximization offers a formal way to learn representations, but optimizing an information objective does not automatically settle whether the resulting representation supports control. This paper investigates that theoretical question.

The authors formalize sufficiency in terms of a representation's ability to support both learning and expressing the optimal policy. They then examine several popular mutual-information objectives using that definition. Two of the objectives can produce insufficient representations under assumptions about the decision process that the authors describe as mild and common.

Experiments in a simulated game with visual observations corroborate the theoretical results. The finding concerns what an objective encourages a representation to retain, beyond the practical difficulty of estimating mutual information from high-dimensional samples. It shows that some popular objectives can lose information needed for optimal control, giving a concrete reason to evaluate representation objectives against policy sufficiency as well as information-based criteria.
neurips-2021-which-mutual-information-re.tldr: Two popular mutual-information objectives can learn representations that fail to preserve enough information for optimal control.

paragraphs: Object detection requires recognizing objects and locating regions in a two-dimensional image. This paper asks how far a Transformer can go when it treats that task primarily as sequence-to-sequence processing, with minimal built-in knowledge of spatial structure. YOLOS is designed to investigate that question through a deliberately minimally modified Vision Transformer.

The model family limits task-specific architectural changes, region priors, and inductive biases. This makes detection a test of how much the general Transformer architecture can accomplish after pretraining. The authors report that pretraining only on ImageNet-1k already yields competitive results on the COCO detection benchmark.

One reported example is YOLOS-Base, directly adapted from the BERT-Base architecture, which achieves 42.0 box AP on COCO validation data. The paper also uses YOLOS to examine the effects and limitations of existing pretraining and model-scaling strategies for vision Transformers. The findings show that competitive detection is possible with relatively little task-specific structural machinery, while leaving the broader role of pretraining and scaling central to the investigation.
neurips-2021-you-only-look-at-one-sequen.tldr: YOLOS achieves competitive object detection with a minimally modified Vision Transformer and limited task-specific spatial assumptions.
